questions.prompt: Explain three differences between a typical photosynthetic plant cell and a bacterial cell.
scheme: 1 · Plant DNA is enclosed in a nucleus; bacterial DNA is not.
2 · The plant cell has chloroplasts; the bacterium does not.
3 · The plant cell has a permanent vacuole; the bacterium does not.

questions.prompt: A cell is 50 μm across. A bacterium is 0.5 μm across. Calculate how many orders of magnitude larger the cell is.
scheme: 2 · 100 = 10², so two orders of magnitude.

questions.prompt: Describe the functions of four structures found in a palisade leaf cell.
scheme: 1 · Nucleus contains genetic material that controls the cell.
2 · Chloroplasts absorb light for photosynthesis.
3 · Cellulose cell wall strengthens/supports the cell.
4 · Permanent vacuole contains cell sap / keeps the cell turgid. Accept mitochondria for respiration, ribosomes for protein synthesis, membrane controls movement of substances.

questions.prompt: Which structure makes proteins?
scheme: Ribosome

questions.prompt: Where is the main bacterial DNA?
scheme: Free in cytoplasm

questions.prompt: Which structure is found in plant cells but not in animal cells?
scheme: Plant cells have cellulose cell walls; animal cells do not.

questions.prompt: What is a plasmid?
options: A small ring of DNA in a bacterium
scheme: Plasmids are small extra rings of DNA found in many bacteria.

questions.prompt: Bacteria are described as prokaryotic because…
options: their genetic material is not in a nucleus
scheme: Prokaryotic cells have no nucleus.

questions.prompt: Which organelle releases most of the energy from aerobic respiration?
scheme: Aerobic respiration takes place mainly in mitochondria.

questions.prompt: A cell image is 54 mm wide at ×1800. Calculate actual width in micrometres.
scheme: 1 · Actual size = image size / magnification.

questions.prompt: A student draws a cheek cell 60 mm wide. The real cell is 60 μm wide. Calculate the magnification of the drawing.
Compare light microscopes and electron microscopes. Explain how electron microscopy has improved our understanding of cells.
scheme: 1 · Electron microscopes have higher magnification.
2 · Electron microscopes have higher resolution / can distinguish two points closer together.
3 · So smaller subcellular structures (e.g. ribosomes, internal structure of mitochondria/chloroplasts) can be seen.
4 · Light microscopes are cheaper/portable and can view living specimens in colour.

questions.prompt: A 20 μm cell appears 40 mm long. Calculate magnification.
What distinguishes two close organelles?
scheme: High resolution

questions.prompt: An image is 12 mm long. The real object is 0.03 mm long. What is the magnification?
How many micrometres are in 1 mm?
Which of these can only be seen clearly with an electron microscope?
scheme: Ribosomes are too small to resolve with a light microscope.

questions.prompt: Write 0.000 005 m in standard form.
scheme: Move the decimal point 6 places: 5 × 10⁻⁶ m.

questions.prompt: Explain three adaptations of a sperm cell for fertilisation.
scheme: 1 · A tail allows movement towards an egg.
2 · Many mitochondria support respiration for movement.
3 · Enzymes in the head help penetrate egg coverings.

questions.prompt: Explain why most animal cells lose the ability to differentiate, while many plant cells keep it.
scheme: 1 · Most animal cells differentiate at an early stage; in adults division is mainly for repair/replacement.
2 · Plants have meristems / continue growing throughout life, so they keep producing new specialised cells.

questions.prompt: Describe how a nerve cell and a root hair cell are each adapted to their function.
scheme: 1 · Nerve cell has a long axon to carry impulses over long distances.
2 · Nerve cell has branched endings/dendrites to connect with many cells.
3 · Root hair cell has a long extension giving a large surface area.
4 · For absorbing water and mineral ions (faster) / many mitochondria for active transport.

questions.prompt: What is differentiation?
scheme: Developing specialised cell structures

questions.prompt: Why is a root hair useful?
scheme: It increases absorbing area

questions.prompt: Why does a sperm cell contain many mitochondria?
options: To store food for the embryo
To release energy for the tail to swim
scheme: Respiration in mitochondria releases energy for swimming.

questions.prompt: Why do root hair cells usually lack chloroplasts?
options: They are underground and receive no light
scheme: No light reaches roots, so chloroplasts would be no use.

questions.prompt: Which describes differentiation?
options: A cell divides into two identical cells
A cell takes in water by osmosis
A cell gains new structures to do a particular job
scheme: Differentiation is the process of a cell becoming specialised.

questions.prompt: What do the branched dendrites of a nerve cell do?
options: Connect with many other nerve cells
scheme: Branched endings let a neurone receive impulses from many cells.

questions.prompt: Describe how the cell cycle produces two genetically identical daughter cells.
scheme: 1 · DNA is replicated before division.
2 · Copies of each chromosome separate to opposite ends and nuclei divide.
3 · Cytoplasm and membrane divide, leaving identical chromosome sets.

questions.prompt: Give two ways a cell prepares for division before mitosis.
scheme: 1 · It grows / increases the number of subcellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria.
2 · It copies/replicates its DNA so each chromosome forms two copies.

questions.prompt: A scientist counts cells in an onion root tip: 380 cells not dividing and 20 cells in mitosis. The cell cycle takes 24 hours. Calculate the time spent in mitosis in minutes, and explain why the root tip is a good place to look.
scheme: 1 · Total cells = 400.
3 · = 72 minutes.
4 · Root tips contain meristem cells that divide frequently.

questions.prompt: Three cells each complete two rounds of division. How many result?
What happens before mitosis?
scheme: DNA is copied

questions.prompt: How many chromosomes are in a human skin cell after mitosis?
scheme: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same.

questions.prompt: Why must DNA be copied before mitosis?
options: So the cell can grow a cell wall
So each daughter cell receives a full set of chromosomes
scheme: Each new cell needs complete genetic information.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a use of mitosis?
scheme: Gametes are produced by meiosis.

questions.prompt: One cell divides by mitosis five times. How many cells result?

b-stem.title: Stem cells: benefits, risks and ethics

questions.prompt: Evaluate embryonic stem cells for replacing damaged nerve tissue.
scheme: 1 · They can differentiate into a wider range of cell types than many adult stem cells.
2 · A biological risk such as infection or uncontrolled division must be considered.
3 · Potential treatment benefit must be weighed against ethical concerns about embryo use.

questions.prompt: Describe how plant meristem tissue can be used to save a rare plant species from extinction.
scheme: 1 · Meristem cells are removed from root/shoot tip.
2 · Grown on a medium/in sterile conditions to form many clones.
3 · Clones are identical, quickly produced and can be replanted/stored.

questions.prompt: Stem cells from embryos could be used to treat type 1 diabetes. Evaluate this use of stem cells.
scheme: 1 · Stem cells could be differentiated into insulin-producing pancreas cells.
2 · This could cure the condition / remove the need for insulin injections.
3 · Therapeutic cloning gives cells that are not rejected by the immune system.
4 · Risk of transferring viral infection from cultured cells.
5 · Risk of cells dividing uncontrollably / tumours.
6 · Ethical/religious objections to using embryos, with a justified conclusion.

questions.prompt: Where are adult human stem cells found?
scheme: Bone marrow

questions.prompt: Why use genetically matched stem cells?
scheme: To reduce rejection

questions.prompt: Where are meristems found in a plant?
scheme: Meristems are regions of active cell division at root and shoot tips.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of therapeutic cloning?
options: Stem cells match the patient so are not rejected
scheme: The cells have the patient's genes.

questions.prompt: Which is a risk of stem-cell treatment?
options: Cells are too large to inject
scheme: Contaminated cultures could transfer viruses.

questions.prompt: Which cell type can adult bone marrow stem cells form?
scheme: Bone marrow stem cells produce a limited range, including blood cells.

questions.prompt: Explain why alveoli exchange gases rapidly.
scheme: 1 · Many alveoli provide a large surface area.
2 · Thin walls give a short diffusion distance.
3 · Ventilation and blood flow maintain concentration gradients.

questions.prompt: Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cube of side 5 mm. Give your answer as a ratio x : 1.
scheme: 1 · Surface area = 6 × 25 = 150 mm².
2 · Volume = 125 mm³.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of villi in the small intestine increases the rate of absorption of digested food.
scheme: 1 · Villi (and microvilli) give a large surface area.
2 · Wall is one cell thick / short diffusion distance.
3 · Rich capillary network carries absorbed molecules away.
4 · Which maintains a steep concentration gradient. Accept many mitochondria for active transport.

questions.prompt: A cube has side 2 cm. Express its surface area to volume ratio as x:1.
scheme: Area 24 cm²; volume 8 cm³; 24:8 = 3:1.

questions.prompt: Which change speeds diffusion?
scheme: A steeper gradient

questions.prompt: What is the SA:V of a 3 cm cube?
scheme: Area 54 cm², volume 27 cm³; 54 ÷ 27 = 2.

questions.prompt: How do fish gills maintain a steep concentration gradient?
options: Blood flows in the opposite direction to water
scheme: Counter-current flow keeps a gradient along the whole gill.

questions.prompt: Which change would halve the rate of diffusion across a membrane?
scheme: Rate is inversely proportional to the diffusion distance.

questions.prompt: Why do single-celled organisms not need a gas exchange system?
options: They have a large surface area to volume ratio
They are too small to need oxygen
scheme: Diffusion across the membrane meets their needs.

questions.prompt: Explain why potato tissue loses mass in concentrated sugar solution.
scheme: 1 · The outside solution is more concentrated than the cell contents.
2 · Water moves out by osmosis across partially permeable cell membranes.
3 · Water loss reduces tissue mass.

questions.prompt: Explain why potato cylinders should be blotted dry before reweighing.
scheme: 1 · Removes surface solution/water.
2 · So the mass measured is only that of the tissue / measurements are comparable.

questions.prompt: Describe a method to find the concentration of sucrose solution with the same water concentration as potato cells.
scheme: 1 · Cut potato cylinders of the same size/with the same borer and length.
2 · Blot and weigh each cylinder.
3 · Place in a range of sucrose concentrations, e.g. 0 to 1.0 mol/dm³.
4 · Leave for the same time at the same temperature.
5 · Remove, blot dry in the same way and reweigh; calculate percentage change.
6 · Plot % change against concentration; where the line crosses zero is the answer.

questions.prompt: A cylinder changes from 4.0 g to 3.6 g. Calculate percentage mass change.
When does water enter a cell by osmosis?
options: Outside is more dilute than inside
scheme: Outside is more dilute than inside

questions.prompt: A potato piece goes from 2.50 g to 2.00 g. What is the percentage change?
Why might a red blood cell burst in pure water?
options: It gains water by osmosis and has no cell wall
scheme: Animal cells have no wall to resist swelling.

questions.prompt: Why is percentage change in mass calculated rather than change in mass?
options: It removes the need for repeats
The pieces had different starting masses
scheme: Percentages allow fair comparison.

questions.prompt: What describes a plant cell that has lost a lot of water?
scheme: Cells that lose water become flaccid.

questions.prompt: Explain why low oxygen availability can reduce mineral uptake by roots.
scheme: 1 · Less oxygen reduces aerobic respiration.
2 · Less energy is available for active transport.
3 · Mineral ions need to move against their concentration gradient.

questions.prompt: Give two differences between diffusion and active transport.
scheme: 1 · Diffusion is down a concentration gradient; active transport is against it.
2 · Diffusion is passive/needs no energy; active transport needs energy from respiration. Accept active transport uses carrier proteins.

questions.prompt: Waterlogged soil contains little oxygen. Explain why plants in waterlogged soil may show signs of mineral deficiency.
scheme: 1 · Root cells receive less oxygen.
2 · So less aerobic respiration / less energy released.
3 · Active transport of mineral ions needs energy.
4 · So fewer mineral ions (e.g. nitrate/magnesium) are absorbed against the gradient.

questions.prompt: Which process requires energy from respiration?
scheme: Active transport

questions.prompt: Mineral concentration is lower in soil than a root cell. Uptake uses…
scheme: Active transport

questions.prompt: What do carrier proteins do in active transport?
options: Move particles across the membrane using energy
scheme: Carrier proteins transport substances against the gradient.

questions.prompt: Why do plants need nitrate ions?
scheme: Nitrate supplies nitrogen for amino acids and proteins.

questions.prompt: Glucose is absorbed from the gut when its concentration in the gut is lower than in the blood. This uses…
scheme: Movement against the gradient requires active transport.

questions.prompt: Which process involves water moving through a partially permeable membrane?
scheme: Osmosis is specific to water.

b-review-cells.title: Cell biology: review and exam practice

questions.prompt: A student views onion cells. Describe how to prepare the slide and focus on the cells.
scheme: 1 · Peel thin layer of onion epidermis and place on slide in a drop of water/iodine.
2 · Lower coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles.
3 · Start with the lowest-power objective.
4 · Use coarse focus then fine focus to get a clear image.

questions.prompt: A cell measures 0.05 mm. A student's drawing of the cell is 25 mm long. Calculate the magnification.
Compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
scheme: 1 · Diffusion: net movement of particles from high to low concentration.
2 · Diffusion is passive / needs no energy.
3 · Osmosis: movement of water through a partially permeable membrane.
4 · From dilute to concentrated solution, passive.
5 · Active transport moves substances against a gradient.
6 · Needs energy from respiration / uses carrier proteins, e.g. mineral uptake by roots.

questions.prompt: Explain why a multicellular organism needs exchange surfaces and a transport system.
scheme: 1 · Large organisms have a small SA:V.
2 · Diffusion alone is too slow over long distances to supply all cells.
3 · Exchange surfaces increase area; transport system carries substances to cells.

questions.prompt: Which structure controls what enters and leaves a cell?
scheme: The membrane is partially permeable.

questions.prompt: An image is 4.8 mm long at × 400. What is the real length?
Which cell type is specialised to carry impulses?
scheme: Nerve cells have long axons.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of mitosis in adults?
scheme: Mitosis gives identical cells.

questions.prompt: Stem cells from embryos can…
scheme: Embryonic stem cells are very versatile.

questions.prompt: Which process moves glucose from a low concentration in the gut into the blood?
scheme: Against a gradient requires energy.

questions.prompt: A cube of side 4 cm has SA:V of…
A potato piece changes from 5.0 g to 5.6 g. Percentage change?
Why do electron microscopes show more detail?
scheme: Resolution determines detail.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT found in a bacterial cell?
scheme: Prokaryotes lack mitochondria.

questions.prompt: Explain how bile assists fat digestion.
scheme: 1 · It neutralises acid, providing alkaline conditions for lipase.
2 · It emulsifies fat into smaller droplets.
3 · This increases surface area available to lipase.

questions.prompt: Give the level of organisation of the stomach and explain your answer.
scheme: 1 · Organ.
2 · It is made of several tissues (e.g. muscle, glandular, epithelial) working together for a function.

questions.prompt: Describe how a protein in food is digested and how the products are used in the body.
scheme: 1 · Protease/pepsin in the stomach begins breaking protein down.
2 · Proteases from the pancreas/small intestine complete digestion to amino acids.
3 · Amino acids are absorbed into the blood through the villi/small intestine wall.
4 · Amino acids are used to build new proteins (e.g. enzymes, muscle).

questions.prompt: Protein digestion produces…
scheme: Amino acids

questions.prompt: Where is bile made?
scheme: Liver

questions.prompt: Which organ produces lipase, protease and amylase?
scheme: The pancreas secretes all three.

questions.prompt: Why does the stomach contain hydrochloric acid?
options: To kill microorganisms and give the low pH for pepsin
scheme: Acid kills pathogens and suits stomach protease.

questions.prompt: What are the products of lipid digestion?
scheme: Lipase breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

questions.prompt: Where is most water absorbed?
scheme: The large intestine absorbs water from undigested material.

questions.prompt: Explain why an enzyme works well at 37°C but poorly at 70°C.
scheme: 1 · High temperature alters protein structure.
2 · The active site changes shape / denatures.
3 · Fewer substrate molecules fit, so fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form.

questions.prompt: Explain why a protease does not digest starch.
scheme: 1 · The active site has a specific shape.
2 · Starch is not complementary to/does not fit the protease active site.

questions.prompt: Describe how to investigate the effect of pH on the rate of starch digestion by amylase.
scheme: 1 · Add iodine drops to each well of a spotting tile.
2 · Mix amylase, starch and a buffer of known pH in a test tube.
3 · Keep at constant temperature in a water bath.
4 · Every 30 s transfer a drop to iodine; record time until iodine stays orange-brown.
5 · Repeat with buffers of different pH (e.g. 5, 6, 7, 8).
6 · Keep volumes/concentrations of starch and amylase the same; repeat and calculate rate = 1/time.

questions.prompt: Starch digestion takes 25 s. Calculate 1/time.
Why is a denatured enzyme less effective?
options: Its active site no longer fits the substrate
scheme: Its active site no longer fits the substrate

questions.prompt: What happens to an enzyme's active site when it denatures?
options: It gets bigger and works faster
It changes shape so the substrate no longer fits
scheme: Denaturing alters the active site shape.

questions.prompt: Starch was all digested after 120 s. What is the relative rate as 1000/time?
In the amylase practical, what does a blue-black colour with iodine show?
scheme: Iodine turns blue-black with starch.

questions.prompt: Why are buffer solutions used in the pH practical?
scheme: Buffers resist pH change.

questions.prompt: A food turns iodine blue-black but heated Benedict’s stays blue. Interpret the results and name a useful control.
scheme: 1 · Starch is detected.
2 · Reducing sugar is not detected under the conditions.
3 · A known sugar solution checks the Benedict’s reagent and heating.

questions.prompt: Name a hazard in the Biuret test and how to reduce the risk.
scheme: 1 · Biuret/sodium hydroxide/copper sulfate is an irritant/corrosive.
2 · Wear eye protection / wash spills from skin immediately.

questions.prompt: Describe how a student could compare the amount of reducing sugar in three fruit juices.
scheme: 1 · Add the same volume of each juice to separate tubes with the same volume of Benedict's.
2 · Heat in a water bath (~75 °C) for the same time.
3 · Compare colours: blue/green/yellow/brick-red.
4 · Use standards of known glucose concentration / a colorimeter to estimate concentration.

questions.prompt: Which indicates protein?
scheme: Lilac Biuret result

questions.prompt: Which test requires a hot water bath?
scheme: Benedict’s

questions.prompt: What is the positive result for the Biuret test?
scheme: Biuret turns lilac with protein.

questions.prompt: Which test must be heated?
scheme: Benedict's is heated in a water bath.

questions.prompt: Which Benedict's colour shows the most reducing sugar?
scheme: Red indicates the highest concentration.

questions.prompt: Why is the food ground and filtered before testing?
options: To make a clear solution of the food
scheme: A clear solution makes colour changes visible.

questions.prompt: Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker muscular wall than the right.
scheme: 1 · It pumps blood around the whole body.
2 · It must generate a higher pressure.
3 · More muscle produces a greater force of contraction.

questions.prompt: Describe the function of the coronary arteries.
scheme: 1 · Supply blood to the heart muscle.
2 · Bringing oxygen/glucose for respiration/contraction.

questions.prompt: Describe the pathway of blood from the vena cava to the aorta, naming the structures it passes through.
scheme: 1 · Vena cava → right atrium → right ventricle.
2 · Pulmonary artery to the lungs, where blood is oxygenated.
3 · Pulmonary vein → left atrium → left ventricle.
4 · Valves prevent backflow; blood leaves through the aorta.

questions.prompt: Which vessel carries blood to lungs?
scheme: Pulmonary artery

questions.prompt: 70 cm³ per beat at 80 beats/min gives what flow?
Which chamber pumps blood into the aorta?
scheme: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the body.

questions.prompt: Why do veins have valves?
options: To prevent backflow of low-pressure blood
scheme: Valves keep blood moving towards the heart.

questions.prompt: Why are capillary walls one cell thick?
options: To give a short diffusion distance
scheme: Thin walls allow rapid exchange.

questions.prompt: Stroke volume 70 cm³, heart rate 72 beats/min. Cardiac output is…
Give a benefit and limitation of a stent and explain why coronary flow matters.
scheme: 1 · A stent improves blood flow through a narrowed artery.
2 · Surgery, infection or clotting presents a risk.
3 · Heart muscle receives more oxygen for aerobic respiration.

questions.prompt: Explain two ways red blood cells are adapted to carry oxygen.
scheme: 1 · Biconcave shape gives large surface area for diffusion.
2 · No nucleus so more space for haemoglobin / contains haemoglobin that binds oxygen.

questions.prompt: Coronary heart disease can be treated with stents, statins or a heart transplant. Evaluate these treatments.
scheme: 1 · Stent opens the narrowed artery and restores blood flow quickly.
2 · Stent surgery has risks, e.g. clots, infection, artery may narrow again.
3 · Statins reduce cholesterol and slow fatty deposit build-up.
4 · Statins must be taken long-term and may have side effects / take time to work.
5 · Transplant needed for heart failure but requires a donor and immunosuppressants.
6 · A justified conclusion linked to severity/situation.

questions.prompt: Which component helps clot blood?
scheme: Platelets

questions.prompt: What does a coronary stent do?
scheme: Keeps a narrowed artery open

questions.prompt: Why do red blood cells have no nucleus?
scheme: This lets them carry more oxygen.

questions.prompt: What do statins do?
scheme: Statins lower LDL cholesterol.

questions.prompt: Which part of blood transports urea?
scheme: Urea is dissolved in plasma.

questions.prompt: A disadvantage of mechanical valves is that…
options: they wear out in a few years
patients need drugs to prevent blood clots
scheme: Mechanical valves increase clot risk.

questions.prompt: Why does a survey linking low exercise and heart disease not prove causation?
scheme: 1 · Correlation alone does not establish cause.
2 · A confounding factor such as age or smoking may affect both.
3 · Further evidence with appropriate comparisons / controls is needed.

questions.prompt: Explain why malignant tumours are more dangerous than benign tumours.
scheme: 1 · Malignant cells invade neighbouring tissues.
2 · They spread in the blood to form secondary tumours elsewhere.

questions.prompt: Discuss how lifestyle factors can affect the risk of non-communicable diseases. Give examples.
scheme: 1 · Smoking increases risk of lung cancer / lung and cardiovascular disease.
2 · Poor diet/obesity increases risk of type 2 diabetes / cardiovascular disease.
3 · Excess alcohol damages the liver / brain.
4 · Risk factors increase probability, not certainty; several factors may interact.

questions.prompt: A risk factor…
scheme: Increases disease probability

questions.prompt: A malignant tumour can…
scheme: Invade tissues and spread

questions.prompt: Which is a non-communicable disease?
scheme: Type 2 diabetes is not passed between people.

questions.prompt: What is a carcinogen?
options: Something that increases the risk of cancer
scheme: Carcinogens, such as tar, increase cancer risk.

questions.prompt: Benign tumours…
options: stay in one place in a membrane
scheme: Benign tumours do not invade other tissues.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of diseases interacting?
scheme: Some viruses can trigger cancer.

questions.prompt: Explain why wind can increase water uptake by a leafy shoot.
scheme: 1 · Wind removes humid air near the leaf.
2 · The steeper gradient increases water-vapour diffusion / transpiration.
3 · Water lost from leaves is replaced through the xylem.

questions.prompt: Explain why most stomata are found on the lower surface of a leaf.
scheme: 1 · The lower surface is cooler/shaded.
2 · So less water is lost by evaporation/transpiration.

questions.prompt: Describe how a potometer could be used to investigate the effect of air movement on the rate of water uptake.
scheme: 1 · Cut shoot under water and fit to potometer under water / seal airtight.
2 · Introduce an air bubble and record distance moved in a set time.
3 · Use a fan at different distances/speeds to change air movement.
4 · Keep light intensity, temperature and the same shoot constant.
5 · Repeat readings and calculate a mean.
6 · Calculate rate = distance (or volume) ÷ time and compare.

questions.prompt: Which tissue transports sugars?
scheme: Phloem

questions.prompt: Why does high humidity reduce transpiration?
scheme: It reduces the water-vapour gradient

questions.prompt: What happens to stomata when guard cells lose water?
scheme: Flaccid guard cells close the stoma.

questions.prompt: Which tissue contains the most chloroplasts?
scheme: Palisade cells are packed with chloroplasts.

questions.prompt: Translocation is the movement of…
scheme: Phloem moves sugars from sources to sinks.

questions.prompt: Why are xylem walls strengthened with lignin?
options: To support the plant and withstand water pressure
scheme: Lignin makes hollow tubes strong.

questions.prompt: Describe how to test a food sample for protein and for starch.
scheme: 1 · Grind food with water and filter.
2 · Add Biuret reagent; lilac/purple shows protein.
3 · Add iodine solution.
4 · Blue-black shows starch.

questions.prompt: Stroke volume is 80 cm³ and heart rate is 75 beats per minute. Calculate cardiac output in dm³/min.
scheme: 2 · = 6.0 dm³/min.

questions.prompt: Explain how the structures of arteries, veins and capillaries are related to their functions.
scheme: 1 · Arteries have thick muscular walls to withstand high pressure.
2 · Elastic fibres stretch and recoil / narrow lumen.
3 · Veins have thin walls and a wide lumen as pressure is low.
4 · Veins have valves to prevent backflow.
5 · Capillaries have walls one cell thick.
6 · Short diffusion distance for exchange with tissues.

questions.prompt: Explain why a high level of saturated fat in the diet increases the risk of a heart attack.
scheme: 1 · Increases blood cholesterol / fatty deposits in coronary arteries.
2 · Arteries narrow so less blood flows to heart muscle.
3 · Less oxygen reaches heart muscle, so cells die / heart attack.

questions.prompt: Which enzyme digests protein?
scheme: Proteases break proteins into amino acids.

questions.prompt: Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs?
scheme: The pulmonary vein returns blood to the heart.

questions.prompt: Which food test needs heating?
scheme: Benedict's test requires a water bath.

questions.prompt: A risk factor for type 2 diabetes is…
scheme: Obesity raises the risk.

questions.prompt: What do platelets do?
scheme: Platelets help form clots.

questions.prompt: Where are stomata mostly found?
scheme: The lower surface is cooler.

questions.prompt: Which factor increases transpiration?
scheme: Warmer air increases evaporation.

questions.prompt: At 70 °C an enzyme stops working because…
options: its active site has changed shape
scheme: High temperature denatures it.

questions.prompt: Which tissue carries water up a plant?
scheme: Xylem carries water and minerals.

questions.prompt: A stent is used to…
scheme: Stents hold arteries open.

questions.prompt: Explain how mosquito nets and removing standing water reduce malaria spread.
scheme: 1 · Nets reduce mosquito bites.
2 · Removing standing water reduces mosquito breeding.
3 · Fewer bites by infected mosquitoes reduce protist transmission.

questions.prompt: Describe the symptoms of HIV and how it is controlled.
scheme: 1 · Initial flu-like symptoms.
2 · Virus attacks immune cells; late stage AIDS when immune system badly damaged.
3 · Controlled with antiretroviral drugs.

questions.prompt: Compare how measles, Salmonella and rose black spot are spread, and suggest one way to reduce the spread of each.
scheme: 1 · Measles spread by droplets / inhalation.
2 · Reduced by vaccination / isolating infected people.
3 · Salmonella spread in food / undercooked food / unhygienic preparation.
4 · Reduced by vaccinating poultry / cooking thoroughly / hygiene.
5 · Rose black spot spread by spores in wind/water.
6 · Reduced by removing/burning infected leaves / fungicides.

questions.prompt: What causes malaria?
options: The mosquito itself as a bacterium
scheme: A protist

questions.prompt: Why can TMV reduce growth?
scheme: Leaf damage reduces photosynthesis

questions.prompt: Which disease is caused by a fungus?
scheme: Rose black spot is a fungal disease.

questions.prompt: How is measles spread?
options: Inhalation of droplets from sneezes and coughs
scheme: Measles is airborne in droplets.

questions.prompt: Why do viruses damage cells?
options: They reproduce inside cells and burst them
scheme: New viruses are released when cells burst.

questions.prompt: A vector is…
options: an organism that carries a pathogen between hosts
scheme: The mosquito is a vector for malaria.

questions.prompt: Explain how vaccination can prevent later disease.
scheme: 1 · Pathogen antigens stimulate a primary immune response safely.
2 · Later exposure triggers faster production of specific antibodies.
3 · The pathogen is destroyed before serious illness develops.

questions.prompt: Describe how the skin and nose defend the body against pathogens.
scheme: 1 · Skin acts as a physical barrier / secretes antimicrobial substances.
2 · Nose has hairs and mucus to trap particles/pathogens.

questions.prompt: Explain why vaccinating a large proportion of a population protects people who are not vaccinated.
scheme: 1 · Vaccinated people are immune / do not become infected.
2 · So fewer people can pass on the pathogen.
3 · The pathogen cannot spread easily through the population.
4 · Unvaccinated people are less likely to meet an infected person (herd immunity).

questions.prompt: What neutralises bacterial toxins?
scheme: Antitoxins

questions.prompt: Why does vaccination help on later exposure?
options: A faster specific immune response occurs
scheme: A faster specific immune response occurs

questions.prompt: What is phagocytosis?
options: A white blood cell engulfing a pathogen
scheme: Phagocytes ingest and digest pathogens.

questions.prompt: What does a vaccine contain?
options: Dead or inactive pathogens or their antigens
Live disease-causing bacteria at full strength
scheme: Vaccines contain harmless antigens.

questions.prompt: How do cilia help defend the body?
options: They move mucus and trapped pathogens up to the throat
scheme: Ciliated cells sweep mucus out of airways.

questions.prompt: Why are antibodies specific?
options: Their shape fits only one antigen
They are made in the stomach
scheme: Each antibody is complementary to one antigen.

questions.prompt: Explain three ways to improve the validity of a drug trial.
scheme: 1 · Random allocation reduces systematic group differences.
2 · An appropriate comparison group helps identify the treatment effect.
3 · Blinding reduces expectation and observer bias.

questions.prompt: Explain why doctors should not prescribe antibiotics for a cold.
scheme: 1 · Colds are caused by viruses / antibiotics do not kill viruses.
2 · Overuse increases the chance of resistant bacteria being selected.

questions.prompt: Explain how a population of antibiotic-resistant bacteria develops.
scheme: 1 · A mutation produces a bacterium that is resistant.
2 · When the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed.
3 · Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce (by binary fission).
4 · The resistance gene is passed on, so the resistant population increases.

questions.prompt: Why do antibiotics not treat viral infections?
options: Viruses lack the bacterial targets and reproduce inside host cells
Viruses are bigger than all bacteria
scheme: Viruses lack the bacterial targets and reproduce inside host cells

questions.prompt: Double-blind means…
options: Neither participants nor assessors know treatment allocation
scheme: Neither participants nor assessors know treatment allocation

questions.prompt: What is tested in phase 1 of a clinical trial?
options: Safety and side effects in healthy volunteers at low doses
scheme: Phase 1 uses low doses in healthy volunteers.

questions.prompt: Which drug came from foxgloves?
scheme: Digitalis is a heart drug from foxgloves.

questions.prompt: Which action helps reduce antibiotic resistance?
options: Completing the full course of antibiotics
Using antibiotics in all animal feed
scheme: Finishing the course kills more bacteria.

questions.prompt: Who discovered penicillin?
scheme: Fleming observed mould killing bacteria in 1928.

b-review-infection.title: Infection and response: review and exam practice

questions.prompt: Describe how malaria is spread and two ways of reducing its spread.
scheme: 1 · Protist carried by mosquito vector, passed on when it bites.
2 · Use insecticide-treated nets / prevent bites.
3 · Remove standing water where mosquitoes breed / insecticides.

questions.prompt: Explain how white blood cells defend the body against pathogens.
scheme: 1 · Phagocytosis: engulf and digest pathogens.
2 · Produce antibodies.
3 · Antibodies specific to antigens on pathogen.
4 · Produce antitoxins to neutralise toxins.

questions.prompt: Describe the stages in developing and testing a new drug.
scheme: 1 · Drug tested on cells/tissues in the lab (preclinical).
2 · Tested on live animals for toxicity and efficacy.
3 · Clinical trials: very low doses on healthy volunteers for side effects.
4 · Then on patients to find optimum dose.
5 · Double-blind trials with a placebo group.
6 · Results peer reviewed before the drug is licensed.

questions.prompt: Explain why vaccinating 90% of a population against measles protects the unvaccinated 10%.
scheme: 1 · Vaccinated people are immune and do not catch or pass on measles.
2 · So the virus cannot spread easily.
3 · Unvaccinated people are less likely to come into contact with it (herd immunity).

questions.prompt: Which disease is caused by a protist?
scheme: Malaria is caused by a protist.

questions.prompt: Tobacco mosaic virus affects…
scheme: TMV infects tobacco and tomato plants.

questions.prompt: What do antitoxins do?
scheme: Antitoxins counteract bacterial toxins.

questions.prompt: Why is a placebo used?
options: To compare the drug with no active treatment
scheme: It controls for psychological effects.

questions.prompt: Which disease is spread by sexual contact and treated with antibiotics?
scheme: Gonorrhoea is bacterial.

questions.prompt: Which body defence uses acid?
scheme: Stomach acid kills pathogens.

questions.prompt: A vaccine causes the body to make…
scheme: Memory cells give long-term immunity.

questions.prompt: Why is it hard to develop drugs against viruses?
options: Viruses live inside cells, so drugs may damage body tissue
scheme: Damaging the virus may damage the host cell.

questions.prompt: What does a double-blind trial prevent?
scheme: Neither group knows who gets the drug.

questions.prompt: Which statement about painkillers is correct?
options: They treat symptoms but do not kill pathogens
scheme: Painkillers relieve symptoms only.

questions.prompt: Explain three uses of glucose in a growing plant.
scheme: 1 · Respiration transfers energy for cellular processes.
2 · Cellulose forms cell walls.
3 · Starch or oils store material, or amino acids are made with nitrate-derived nitrogen.

questions.prompt: Write the balanced symbol equation for photosynthesis.
scheme: 1 · 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂: correct formulae.
2 · Correctly balanced.

questions.prompt: Explain how a plant obtains the substances it needs to make glucose and protein.
scheme: 1 · Carbon dioxide diffuses into the leaf through stomata.
2 · Water is absorbed by root hair cells (osmosis) and travels in xylem.
3 · Light absorbed by chlorophyll.
4 · Nitrate ions absorbed from soil by active transport to make amino acids/protein.

questions.prompt: Which gas enters for photosynthesis?
scheme: Carbon dioxide

questions.prompt: Why are nitrates needed?
options: For amino acid and protein synthesis
scheme: For amino acid and protein synthesis

questions.prompt: What is the chemical formula of glucose?
scheme: Glucose is C₆H₁₂O₆.

questions.prompt: Why is photosynthesis endothermic?
options: Energy is transferred from the environment (light) to the reaction
scheme: Light energy is taken in.

questions.prompt: Why is a leaf warmed in ethanol before testing for starch?
options: To remove chlorophyll so the colour change can be seen
scheme: Ethanol decolourises the leaf.

questions.prompt: Which substance is made from glucose to strengthen cell walls?
scheme: Cellulose forms plant cell walls.

questions.prompt: Suggest three improvements to a pondweed experiment comparing light levels.
scheme: 1 · Control temperature to avoid lamp heating as a confounder.
2 · Keep plant size and carbon dioxide supply consistent.
3 · Collect gas volume over equal periods and repeat for means.

questions.prompt: Explain why a beaker of water is placed between the lamp and the pondweed.
scheme: 1 · Absorbs heat from the lamp.
2 · So temperature stays constant / temperature is a control variable.

questions.prompt: A student finds the rate of photosynthesis at 10, 20, 30 and 40 cm from a lamp. Describe how the results would be presented and analysed to reach a conclusion.
scheme: 1 · Calculate mean volume/rate at each distance from repeats.
2 · Plot rate (y) against distance or light intensity (x).
3 · Draw a line/curve of best fit and identify anomalies.
4 · Conclusion: rate decreases as distance increases / increases with light intensity up to a point.

questions.prompt: 18 cm³ oxygen is collected in 6 minutes. Calculate rate.
What does a horizontal oxygen-rate curve indicate?
scheme: A constant rate

questions.prompt: Why is sodium hydrogencarbonate added to the water?
scheme: It releases CO₂ for photosynthesis.

questions.prompt: Why is the pondweed left for a few minutes before each reading?
options: To adjust to the new light intensity
scheme: This lets the rate become steady.

questions.prompt: What is the independent variable in this practical?
scheme: Distance is changed deliberately.

questions.prompt: Why is counting bubbles less accurate than collecting gas?
scheme: Volume is measured directly by gas collection.

questions.prompt: Extra light has no effect but extra carbon dioxide raises rate. Explain and give an economic implication.
scheme: 1 · Light is not limiting under the tested conditions.
2 · Carbon dioxide is limiting because adding it raises rate.
3 · Extra lighting alone adds cost without improving production.

questions.prompt: Light intensity at 15 cm is 36 units. Calculate the intensity at 45 cm.
A farmer grows lettuces in a greenhouse in winter. Explain how the farmer could increase yield and why the extra cost may not always be worthwhile.
scheme: 1 · Increase temperature with heaters.
2 · Add artificial light / extend daylight hours.
3 · Add carbon dioxide / use paraffin heaters.
4 · Increasing a factor only helps if it is the limiting factor.
5 · Once another factor limits, further increases give no extra growth.
6 · Profit only rises if value of extra yield exceeds extra cost of fuel/electricity.

questions.prompt: Intensity is 80 units at 10 cm. Estimate intensity at 20 cm.
scheme: Distance doubles, so intensity divides by 4.

questions.prompt: Revenue rises £600 and costs rise £750. Profit changes by…
scheme: A £150 decrease

questions.prompt: Light intensity at 10 cm is 100 units. What is it at 50 cm?
On the steep rising part of a light-intensity curve, what limits the rate?
scheme: Increasing light still increases rate there.

questions.prompt: Why does a paraffin heater help two ways in a greenhouse?
options: It warms the air and releases carbon dioxide
scheme: Burning paraffin gives heat and CO₂.

questions.prompt: Why can very high temperatures reduce the rate of photosynthesis?
scheme: Photosynthesis is enzyme controlled.

questions.prompt: Compare anaerobic respiration in muscles and yeast.
scheme: 1 · Both break down glucose without oxygen.
2 · Muscles produce lactic acid; yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide.
3 · Both transfer less energy per glucose than aerobic respiration.

questions.prompt: Write the balanced symbol equation for aerobic respiration.
scheme: 1 · C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O: correct formulae.
2 · Correctly balanced.

questions.prompt: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in humans.
scheme: 1 · Aerobic needs oxygen; anaerobic does not.
2 · Aerobic produces carbon dioxide and water; anaerobic produces lactic acid.
3 · Aerobic transfers much more energy per glucose.
4 · Aerobic occurs in mitochondria; anaerobic in the cytoplasm / glucose only partly broken down in anaerobic.

questions.prompt: Aerobic respiration produces…
scheme: Carbon dioxide and water

questions.prompt: Why is less energy transferred anaerobically?
scheme: Glucose breakdown is incomplete

questions.prompt: Where does most aerobic respiration take place?
scheme: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration.

questions.prompt: What are the products of fermentation in yeast?
scheme: Yeast produces ethanol and CO₂ anaerobically.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT a use of energy from respiration?
scheme: Diffusion is passive.

questions.prompt: Respiration is exothermic. This means it…
scheme: Exothermic reactions release energy.

questions.prompt: Explain why heart rate and breathing rate increase during exercise.
scheme: 1 · Muscle energy demand / respiration increases.
2 · Faster breathing supplies oxygen and removes carbon dioxide.
3 · Faster circulation delivers oxygen and glucose to muscles.

questions.prompt: Give two variables that should be controlled when comparing the effect of exercise on heart rate in different students.
scheme: 1 · Type/intensity of exercise.
2 · Duration of exercise / time of measurement / same resting conditions.

questions.prompt: Explain the changes that happen in the body during vigorous exercise and why they happen.
scheme: 1 · Muscles respire faster so need more energy.
2 · Heart rate increases to deliver more oxygen and glucose.
3 · Breathing rate and depth increase.
4 · So more oxygen absorbed and more carbon dioxide removed.
5 · If oxygen supply is insufficient, anaerobic respiration produces lactic acid.
6 · Lactic acid causes fatigue / oxygen debt after exercise.

questions.prompt: Why does heart rate rise in exercise?
options: To turn oxygen into lactic acid
To deliver oxygen and glucose faster
scheme: To deliver oxygen and glucose faster

questions.prompt: Metabolism means…
options: All reactions in a cell or organism
scheme: All reactions in a cell or organism

questions.prompt: Resting breathing rate 14/min rises to 21/min. Percentage increase?
Why does breath volume increase during exercise?
options: More oxygen enters and more CO₂ is removed
scheme: Deeper breaths increase gas exchange.

questions.prompt: What forms when excess amino acids are broken down?
scheme: Deamination in the liver forms urea.

questions.prompt: A fitter person usually…
options: returns to resting heart rate faster
has a higher resting heart rate
scheme: Recovery time indicates fitness.

questions.prompt: Explain elevated oxygen uptake after intense exercise.
scheme: 1 · Anaerobic respiration has caused lactic acid accumulation.
2 · Blood carries it to the liver for conversion back to glucose.
3 · Extra oxygen is needed during recovery, forming oxygen debt.

questions.prompt: Explain why the heart rate stays high for several minutes after exercise.
scheme: 1 · Blood carries lactic acid to the liver.
2 · And delivers oxygen needed to convert lactic acid / repay oxygen debt.

questions.prompt: Two athletes run the same distance. Athlete A has an oxygen debt of 2 L; athlete B has an oxygen debt of 5 L. Explain what this shows.
scheme: 1 · Athlete B respired anaerobically more.
2 · So produced more lactic acid.
3 · More oxygen needed to convert lactic acid to glucose in the liver.
4 · Athlete A is likely fitter / delivers oxygen to muscles more efficiently.

questions.prompt: Additional uptake averages 2 L/min for 3 min. Calculate extra oxygen.
Where is lactic acid converted back to glucose?
scheme: Liver

questions.prompt: What is converted to glucose in the liver after exercise?
scheme: Liver converts lactic acid back to glucose.

questions.prompt: Why does breathing remain fast after exercise?
options: To supply oxygen to repay the oxygen debt
scheme: Extra oxygen removes lactic acid.

questions.prompt: Extra uptake is 1.5 L/min for 4 minutes. Oxygen debt is…
What causes muscle fatigue during intense exercise?
scheme: Lactic acid accumulates.

questions.prompt: A student counts 48 bubbles in 4 minutes. Calculate the rate in bubbles per minute and give one reason why measuring volume is better.
scheme: 2 · bubbles per minute.
3 · Bubbles may be different sizes, so volume is more accurate.

questions.prompt: Compare aerobic respiration in humans with anaerobic respiration in yeast.
scheme: 1 · Aerobic needs oxygen; anaerobic in yeast does not.
2 · Aerobic products: CO₂ and water; yeast: ethanol and CO₂.
3 · Aerobic releases more energy per glucose.
4 · Aerobic mainly in mitochondria; anaerobic in cytoplasm.

questions.prompt: Describe how to investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis using pondweed.
scheme: 1 · Put pondweed in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution under a funnel/in a boiling tube.
2 · Place a lamp at a measured distance, e.g. 10 cm.
3 · Leave to acclimatise, then count bubbles / collect gas for a set time.
4 · Repeat at different distances.
5 · Control temperature using a water bath/heat shield; same pondweed.
6 · Repeat and calculate mean rate; plot rate against distance or 1/d².

questions.prompt: Explain why a gardener's glasshouse crop grows faster when the air is warmer, up to a point.
scheme: 1 · Photosynthesis is controlled by enzymes.
2 · Warmer temperatures increase enzyme activity / rate up to the optimum.
3 · Above the optimum, enzymes denature so rate falls.

questions.prompt: What are the reactants of photosynthesis?
scheme: CO₂ + H₂O → glucose + O₂.

questions.prompt: Which substance stores glucose in plants?
scheme: Starch is insoluble storage.

questions.prompt: Fermentation in yeast produces…
scheme: Used in brewing and baking.

questions.prompt: Why does heart rate increase during exercise?
options: To reduce CO₂ in muscles only
To supply more oxygen and glucose to muscles
scheme: Muscles respire faster.

questions.prompt: Which is a limiting factor of photosynthesis?
scheme: Temperature, light and CO₂ are limiting factors.

questions.prompt: Lactic acid is converted back to glucose in the…
scheme: The liver processes lactic acid.

questions.prompt: Respiration is described as exothermic because…
options: it transfers energy to the surroundings
scheme: Energy is released.

questions.prompt: In the pondweed practical, the volume of gas measures…
scheme: Oxygen is a product.

questions.prompt: Which molecule is made from glucose and nitrate ions?
scheme: Nitrogen is needed for amino acids.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct?
scheme: Respiration is continuous.

questions.prompt: Describe withdrawal of a hand from a hot object.
scheme: 1 · A receptor detects the stimulus and a sensory neurone carries an impulse to the CNS.
2 · Signals pass across synapses via a relay neurone to a motor neurone.
3 · A muscle contracts to withdraw the hand.

questions.prompt: Explain why a reflex action is faster than a voluntary response.
scheme: 1 · The pathway does not involve the conscious part of the brain / goes through spinal cord.
2 · Fewer neurones/synapses, so shorter pathway.

questions.prompt: Describe what happens at a synapse and explain why impulses can only travel in one direction.
scheme: 1 · Impulse arrives at end of neurone and neurotransmitter is released.
2 · Chemical diffuses across the gap.
3 · Binds to receptors on the next neurone, triggering an impulse.
4 · Only the first neurone releases transmitter / receptors only on the next neurone, so one direction.

questions.prompt: Which neurone carries information towards the CNS?
scheme: Sensory

questions.prompt: An effector is…
options: A muscle or gland producing a response
scheme: A muscle or gland producing a response

questions.prompt: How does an impulse cross a synapse?
options: A chemical diffuses across the gap
scheme: Neurotransmitters diffuse across the synapse.

questions.prompt: Which is an effector?
scheme: Effectors are muscles or glands.

questions.prompt: Why are reflexes important?
options: They are fast and protect the body
scheme: Reflexes respond rapidly to danger.

questions.prompt: Where are relay neurones found?
scheme: Relay neurones link sensory and motor neurones in the CNS.

questions.prompt: Explain three controls in a ruler-drop comparison of distraction.
scheme: 1 · Use consistent hand and ruler starting positions.
2 · Randomise or counterbalance condition order.
3 · Repeat trials across participants and compare means.

questions.prompt: Suggest why the mean of several trials gives a better estimate of reaction time than a single trial.
scheme: 1 · Reduces the effect of random error/variation.
2 · Anomalous results can be identified and excluded.

questions.prompt: Plan an investigation to find whether listening to music affects reaction time.
scheme: 1 · Use ruler-drop: catcher's thumb at zero, ruler dropped without warning.
2 · Record catch distance and convert to time.
3 · Test each person with and without music.
4 · Control same hand, same ruler, same dropper, same position/practice.
5 · Repeat several times and calculate means; use many participants.
6 · Obtain consent; randomise order to reduce practice effects.

questions.prompt: Fall distances are 12, 14 and 16 cm. Calculate the mean.
Which reduces order bias?
scheme: Randomising condition order

questions.prompt: What is the dependent variable in a ruler-drop test?
options: Distance the ruler falls before being caught
scheme: Catch distance is measured.

questions.prompt: Why should the dropper give no warning?
options: So the catcher reacts to sight, not anticipation
scheme: Warnings allow prediction.

questions.prompt: Why should several practice trials be allowed?
options: To reduce the effect of learning during the test
scheme: Practice effects can bias results.

questions.prompt: Catch distances of 15, 17, 16 and 32 cm. Which is anomalous?
scheme: 32 cm is far from the others.

questions.prompt: Explain how insulin lowers blood glucose after a meal.
scheme: 1 · The pancreas detects raised glucose and secretes insulin.
2 · Glucose moves from blood into cells.
3 · Excess glucose is converted to glycogen in liver and muscle.

questions.prompt: Give two differences between nervous and hormonal responses.
scheme: 1 · Nervous: electrical impulses; hormonal: chemicals in blood.
2 · Nervous fast and short-lived; hormonal slower and longer-lasting.

questions.prompt: Compare the causes and treatment of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
scheme: 1 · Type 1: pancreas produces too little insulin.
2 · Type 1 treated by insulin injections.
3 · Type 2: body cells do not respond to insulin.
4 · Type 2 treated with carbohydrate-controlled diet/exercise; obesity is a risk factor.

questions.prompt: Which gland secretes insulin?
scheme: Pancreas

questions.prompt: Glycogen is…
scheme: A storage carbohydrate

questions.prompt: Which gland is known as the master gland?
scheme: Pituitary hormones control other glands.

questions.prompt: Type 2 diabetes is mainly treated by…
scheme: Lifestyle change is first-line treatment.

questions.prompt: What is a risk factor for type 2 diabetes?
scheme: Obesity is strongly linked.

questions.prompt: How do hormones travel to target organs?
scheme: Endocrine glands secrete into the blood.

questions.prompt: Explain correction of low blood glucose by negative feedback.
scheme: 1 · The pancreas detects the fall and releases glucagon.
2 · Liver glycogen is converted to glucose and released into blood.
3 · Glucagon secretion falls as glucose returns towards normal.

questions.prompt: Explain why adrenaline release is useful in a dangerous situation.
scheme: 1 · Increases heart rate / blood flow.
2 · More oxygen and glucose delivered to muscles and brain for fight or flight.

questions.prompt: Explain how insulin and glucagon interact to keep blood glucose concentration within normal limits.
scheme: 1 · After a meal, glucose rises and is detected by the pancreas.
2 · Pancreas secretes insulin.
3 · Insulin causes cells to take up glucose and liver/muscles convert glucose to glycogen.
4 · When glucose falls, pancreas secretes glucagon.
5 · Glucagon causes liver to convert glycogen to glucose, released into blood.
6 · Each response reverses the change — negative feedback.

questions.prompt: Which raises low blood glucose?
scheme: Glucagon

questions.prompt: Negative feedback…
scheme: Opposes the original change

questions.prompt: Glucagon causes the liver to…
scheme: Glucagon raises blood glucose.

questions.prompt: Which hormone increases heart rate in a fight-or-flight response?
scheme: Adrenaline prepares the body for action.

questions.prompt: Which hormone stimulates the thyroid gland?
scheme: Thyroid-stimulating hormone from the pituitary.

questions.prompt: Thyroxine mainly controls…
scheme: Thyroxine regulates metabolic rate.

questions.prompt: Compare a condom and a hormonal implant.
scheme: 1 · Condoms form a barrier preventing sperm reaching eggs.
2 · Implants release hormones to inhibit egg maturation or release without action at every intercourse.
3 · Condoms reduce some STI transmission; implants alone do not.

questions.prompt: Give the roles of FSH and LH in the menstrual cycle.
scheme: 1 · FSH causes an egg to mature in the ovary.
2 · LH stimulates release of the egg / ovulation.

questions.prompt: Evaluate hormonal and non-hormonal methods of contraception.
scheme: 1 · Hormonal methods (pill, implant) very effective when used correctly.
2 · Implants/injections last months/years, so no need to remember daily.
3 · But may cause side effects, e.g. mood changes / blood clot risk.
4 · Hormonal methods do not protect against STIs.
5 · Condoms protect against STIs and have no hormonal side effects.
6 · But are less effective with typical use / can tear; a justified conclusion.

questions.prompt: Which triggers ovulation?
scheme: LH

questions.prompt: Which can also reduce STI transmission?
scheme: Condom

questions.prompt: Which hormone causes the uterus lining to grow?
scheme: Oestrogen rebuilds the lining.

questions.prompt: Where is FSH made?
scheme: FSH comes from the pituitary.

questions.prompt: How does the combined pill prevent pregnancy?
options: Oestrogen inhibits FSH so eggs do not mature
scheme: Inhibiting FSH stops egg maturation.

questions.prompt: Which method is permanent?
scheme: Sterilisation cuts or ties tubes.

questions.prompt: Explain hormone use in IVF and give one limitation.
scheme: 1 · FSH/LH stimulate maturation of several eggs / ovulation.
2 · Eggs are collected and fertilised in a laboratory before embryo transfer.
3 · A valid limitation includes variable success, treatment stress or multiple births.

questions.prompt: Explain why progesterone levels fall at the end of the cycle if the egg is not fertilised, and the effect of this.
scheme: 1 · Corpus luteum breaks down so progesterone production stops.
2 · Uterus lining is no longer maintained and breaks down (menstruation).

questions.prompt: Describe the stages of IVF treatment and evaluate its use.
scheme: 1 · Mother given FSH and LH to stimulate maturation of several eggs.
2 · Eggs collected from the mother and fertilised by sperm in the lab.
3 · Fertilised eggs develop into embryos; one or two inserted into the uterus.
4 · Benefit: allows infertile couples to have children.
5 · Drawbacks: low success rate / expensive / emotionally and physically stressful.
6 · Multiple births risk / ethical concerns about unused embryos.

questions.prompt: What stimulates the LH surge in the model?
scheme: Increased oestrogen

questions.prompt: Where does fertilisation happen in IVF?
scheme: Laboratory

questions.prompt: Which hormone maintains the uterus lining after ovulation?
scheme: Progesterone keeps the lining.

questions.prompt: In IVF, why are women given FSH and LH?
options: To stimulate several eggs to mature
scheme: More eggs can be collected.

questions.prompt: Which is a risk of IVF?
scheme: Several embryos may implant.

questions.prompt: What inhibits FSH after an egg matures?
scheme: Oestrogen inhibits FSH.

b-review-homeostasis.title: Homeostasis and response: review and exam practice

questions.prompt: Describe the pathway of a reflex arc when you touch a sharp pin.

questions.prompt: Explain how blood glucose concentration is controlled after a meal containing carbohydrate.
scheme: 1 · Blood glucose rises; detected by the pancreas.

scheme: 1 · Hormonal pill/implant inhibits FSH so no eggs mature; highly effective.
2 · Implants last for years; no need to remember daily.
3 · Hormonal methods may have side effects and do not protect against STIs.
4 · Condoms are a barrier and protect against STIs.
5 · Condoms can split / less effective with typical use.
6 · Justified conclusion depending on needs.

questions.prompt: Give two differences between type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
scheme: 1 · Type 1: pancreas makes too little insulin; type 2: cells do not respond to insulin.
2 · Type 1 treated with insulin injections; type 2 with diet and exercise.

questions.prompt: Which neurone carries impulses to an effector?
scheme: Motor neurones connect to muscles or glands.

questions.prompt: What does the pancreas release when blood glucose is high?
scheme: Insulin lowers glucose.

questions.prompt: What is the role of a receptor?
scheme: Receptors detect changes.

questions.prompt: Which hormone stimulates sperm production?
scheme: Testosterone is made in the testes.

questions.prompt: Type 1 diabetes is caused by…
options: the pancreas producing too little insulin
scheme: Type 1 involves little insulin.

questions.prompt: Which is a barrier method of contraception?
scheme: Condoms prevent sperm reaching the egg.

questions.prompt: Which gland releases adrenaline?
scheme: Adrenal glands are above the kidneys.

questions.prompt: Hormones are carried by…
scheme: Endocrine glands secrete into blood.

questions.prompt: Which hormone causes ovulation?
scheme: An LH surge releases the egg.

questions.prompt: A reflex is faster than a voluntary action because…
options: it does not involve the conscious brain
scheme: The pathway is shorter.

questions.prompt: Explain maintenance of chromosome number across generations.

questions.prompt: Give two differences between mitosis and meiosis.
scheme: 1 · Mitosis produces two cells; meiosis four.
2 · Mitosis cells genetically identical with full chromosome number; meiosis cells different with half.

questions.prompt: Describe what happens during meiosis and explain why gametes need half the normal number of chromosomes.
scheme: 1 · Genetic information is copied.

questions.prompt: Body cells have 30 chromosomes. How many in a normal gamete?
scheme: Meiosis halves 30 to 15.

questions.prompt: What restores the full chromosome number?
scheme: Fertilisation

questions.prompt: How many cells are produced from one cell by meiosis?
scheme: Meiosis involves two divisions.

questions.prompt: Where does meiosis take place in humans?
scheme: Gametes are made in the reproductive organs.

questions.prompt: What are the gametes in flowering plants?
scheme: Pollen carries the male gamete.

questions.prompt: After fertilisation the zygote divides by…
scheme: Growth uses mitosis.

questions.prompt: Give a medical use and limitation of genome knowledge.
scheme: 1 · It can identify variants associated with an inherited disorder.
2 · This can support diagnosis, risk assessment or treatment research.
3 · Variants may not determine outcome because other genes and environment contribute.

questions.prompt: Describe the relationship between chromosomes, DNA and genes.
scheme: 1 · Chromosomes are made of DNA.
2 · A gene is a small section of DNA on a chromosome that codes for a protein.

questions.prompt: Explain how understanding the human genome could help in medicine and give two concerns.
scheme: 1 · Identify genes linked to diseases.
2 · Allows early treatment/screening or development of targeted treatments.
3 · Concern: discrimination by insurers/employers.
4 · Concern: anxiety from knowing risk / results not certain / privacy.

questions.prompt: A genome is…
options: All genetic material of an organism
scheme: All genetic material of an organism

questions.prompt: A gene codes for…
options: An amino acid sequence in a protein
scheme: An amino acid sequence in a protein

questions.prompt: What shape is a DNA molecule?
scheme: Two strands twist into a double helix.

questions.prompt: DNA is described as a polymer because it…
options: is made of many repeating units
scheme: DNA is made of many nucleotides.

questions.prompt: Which is a use of genome knowledge?
scheme: DNA comparisons show ancestry.

questions.prompt: Which is a concern about genetic testing?
scheme: Personal genetic data raise ethical issues.

questions.prompt: Two unaffected parents have a child with a recessive disorder. Explain their genotypes in the single-gene model.

3 · Both are heterozygous carriers.

questions.prompt: Define the terms homozygous and heterozygous.
scheme: 1 · Homozygous: two identical alleles of a gene.
2 · Heterozygous: two different alleles of a gene.

questions.prompt: Discuss the benefits and ethical issues of screening embryos for genetic disorders.
scheme: 1 · Embryos tested for alleles of disorders, e.g. cystic fibrosis.
2 · Benefit: avoids suffering from serious genetic disorders.
3 · Benefit: may reduce lifelong treatment costs.
4 · Issue: expensive / not always accurate.
5 · Issue: destruction of embryos / implies disabled people less valued.
6 · Issue: fear of designer babies; regulated by law.

questions.prompt: Heterozygous means…
scheme: Two different alleles

questions.prompt: Why can a recessive carrier be unaffected?
options: A dominant allele masks the recessive effect
scheme: A dominant allele masks the recessive effect

questions.prompt: A person with genotype Dd has polydactyly. The allele is…

questions.prompt: What are the sex chromosomes of a human male?
scheme: Males are XY.

questions.prompt: Phenotype means…
scheme: Phenotype is what is expressed.

questions.prompt: Why can two healthy parents have a child with cystic fibrosis?
options: Both are carriers of the recessive allele
It is caused by a virus

questions.prompt: Antibiotic resistance spreads because…

questions.prompt: What is extension?

questions.prompt: How should an unexpected reading be handled?

How far does a car travel in 12 s at 25 m/s?

scheme: The distance does not change.

questions.prompt: Making a soluble saltA student makes copper sulfate crystals using dilute sulfuric acid and copper oxide. Describe how to make pure, dry copper sulfate crystals from these starting materials.
scheme: 1 · Warm dilute sulfuric acid gently using suitable safe heating; wear eye protection.
2 · Add copper oxide in small portions while stirring.
3 · Continue adding until solid remains/no more reacts, showing excess oxide.
4 · Filter to remove excess unreacted copper oxide.
5 · Heat filtrate gently to evaporate some water, then allow to cool so crystals form.
6 · Filter crystals and dry between filter papers/in a warm place. Do not credit boiling to dryness.
questions.note: Award one mark per distinct valid step, maximum 6.

questions.prompt: Making a soluble saltA student makes copper sulfate crystals using dilute sulfuric acid and copper oxide. Explain why an excess of copper oxide is added and then filtered off.

questions.prompt: Electromagnetic radiationElectromagnetic waves travel at 300000000 m/s in a vacuum. A radio wave has frequency 100000000 Hz. Use v = fλ. State two features shared by all electromagnetic waves.

Measuring waves on a stringA vibrator produces waves along a string. The wavelength is measured as 0.80 m and the frequency is 12 Hz. Use v = fλ. State why measuring across several wavelengths is better than measuring one.
scheme: 1 · Reduces relative/percentage uncertainty in total length (1).

questions.prompt: Measuring waves on a stringA vibrator produces waves along a string. The wavelength is measured as 0.80 m and the frequency is 12 Hz. Use v = fλ. Describe a safe method to investigate how changing frequency affects wavelength when wave speed is kept approximately constant.

scheme: 1 · From north pole to south pole (1).

questions.prompt: Magnets and electromagnetsA coil of insulated wire is wrapped around an iron nail and connected to a low-voltage supply. Describe how a compass can be used to plot a magnetic field.

3 · Repeat from different starting positions and add arrows (1).

questions.prompt: Exchange surfaces and cell sizeModel cells are cubes. Cube A has side length 1 mm; cube B has side length 3 mm. Surface area of a cube = 6 × side²; volume = side³. A micrograph is 72 mm wide at ×600. Calculate the real width in micrometres.

scheme: 1 · Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient; diffusion is down it (1).
2 · Active transport requires energy from respiration; diffusion does not (1).

scheme: 1 · Valid systematic error such as consistently leaving surface solution on cylinders before weighing (1).

questions.prompt: Heart disease and evidenceIn a study, 18 of 300 people in group A developed heart disease, compared with 45 of 300 in group B. Group A took part in an exercise programme. scheme: 1 · Double circulation sends blood to lungs and then to body.

questions.prompt: Infection and immunityA viral infection causes symptoms in some patients. A doctor explains that antibiotics will not cure the viral infection. Explain why antibiotics are ineffective against viruses.
scheme: 1 · Antibiotics target bacterial structures/processes (1).

questions.prompt: Infection and immunityA viral infection causes symptoms in some patients. A doctor explains that antibiotics will not cure the viral infection. Describe three ways white blood cells defend the body against pathogens.
scheme: 1 · Phagocytosis/engulfing pathogens (1).

scheme: 1 · Mutation produces a resistant bacterium/variation already exists (1).

questions.prompt: Infection and immunityA viral infection causes symptoms in some patients. A doctor explains that antibiotics will not cure the viral infection. Give two reasons why a new drug is tested before use in patients.
scheme: 1 · Determine toxicity/safety (1).
2 · Determine effectiveness or an appropriate dose (1).

questions.prompt: Limiting photosynthesisAt a fixed temperature, a plant absorbs 2.4 mg of carbon dioxide in 4 minutes at light setting A and 4.8 mg in 4 minutes at setting B. Doubling the light again gives no further increase. Calculate the carbon dioxide uptake rate at setting B.

Limiting photosynthesisAt a fixed temperature, a plant absorbs 2.4 mg of carbon dioxide in 4 minutes at light setting A and 4.8 mg in 4 minutes at setting B. Doubling the light again gives no further increase. Explain why doubling light beyond B may give no further increase.

questions.prompt: Metabolism and exerciseA person runs at increasing speed until oxygen delivery can no longer meet demand. Explain the relationship between respiration and metabolism.
scheme: 1 · Respiration transfers energy from glucose (1).

questions.prompt: Metabolism and exerciseA person runs at increasing speed until oxygen delivery can no longer meet demand. Explain why anaerobic respiration leads to muscle fatigue and an oxygen debt.
scheme: 1 · Glucose is incompletely broken down to lactic acid (1).
2 · Lactic acid accumulation contributes to fatigue (1).

questions.prompt: Metabolism and exerciseA person runs at increasing speed until oxygen delivery can no longer meet demand. Describe how lactic acid is processed after exercise.

questions.prompt: Metabolism and exerciseA person runs at increasing speed until oxygen delivery can no longer meet demand. Compare anaerobic respiration in yeast with that in muscles.
scheme: 1 · Yeast produces ethanol and carbon dioxide; muscles produce lactic acid (1).

scheme: 1 · Impulse triggers release of a neurotransmitter (1).

questions.prompt: Comparing nervous and hormonal controlConditionReaction time 1 / msReaction time 2 / msReaction time 3 / msQuiet210220230Distraction270280290 Compare nervous and hormonal coordination.
scheme: 1 · Nervous signals travel along neurones; hormones are carried in blood (1).

questions.prompt: Negative feedbackA fasting person has falling blood glucose concentration. For the thyroxine question, use this information: the pituitary releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine. Explain how glucagon restores blood glucose concentration.
scheme: 1 · Pancreas detects low blood glucose/releases glucagon (1).

questions.prompt: Negative feedbackA fasting person has falling blood glucose concentration. For the thyroxine question, use this information: the pituitary releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine. Explain why this is negative feedback.

questions.prompt: Negative feedbackA fasting person has falling blood glucose concentration. For the thyroxine question, use this information: the pituitary releases TSH, which stimulates the thyroid gland to release thyroxine. Explain how adrenaline prepares the body for action.

questions.prompt: Reproductive hormone interactionsA clinic treats some cases of infertility with hormones. Success is not guaranteed. State the roles of FSH and LH during fertility treatment.
scheme: 1 · FSH stimulates maturation of eggs (1).

questions.prompt: Reproductive hormone interactionsA clinic treats some cases of infertility with hormones. Success is not guaranteed. Explain how oestrogen and progesterone help regulate the menstrual cycle.
scheme: 1 · Oestrogen stimulates rebuilding uterus lining (1).

scheme: 1 · Can enable an infertile couple to have a child (1).

scheme: 1 · Meiosis halves chromosome number in gametes (1).

questions.prompt: Meiosis and inheritanceA recessive allele a causes a genetic condition. A carrier Aa has a child with a person aa who has the condition. Explain why siblings can have different phenotypes even with the same parents.
scheme: 1 · Sexual reproduction produces different combinations of parental alleles (1).

questions.prompt: Meiosis and inheritanceA recessive allele a causes a genetic condition. A carrier Aa has a child with a person aa who has the condition. Evaluate using the result of this cross to predict the outcomes for exactly two children.
scheme: 1 · Probability applies independently to each conception (1).

questions.prompt: Antibiotic resistance and genetic engineeringA hospital finds that an increasing proportion of bacteria are resistant to an antibiotic. Explain how resistance becomes more common and how prescribing decisions can slow this process.
scheme: 1 · Random mutation creates an allele giving resistance/variation already exists.

4 · Resistant bacteria survive and reproduce rapidly.
5 · Resistance allele is passed to offspring, increasing its frequency.
6 · Prescribing antibiotics only when needed reduces selection pressure. Accept completion of the prescribed course as an alternative control, with a correct explanation.
questions.note: Award one mark per distinct valid linked point, maximum 6.

questions.prompt: Antibiotic resistance and genetic engineeringA hospital finds that an increasing proportion of bacteria are resistant to an antibiotic. Describe how bacteria can be genetically engineered to produce human insulin.
scheme: 1 · Human insulin gene is isolated using enzymes (1).
2 · Gene inserted into a vector/plasmid using enzymes (1).
3 · Vector introduces gene into bacteria (1).
4 · Modified bacteria are grown and express the gene to produce insulin, which is collected/purified (1).

questions.prompt: Interdependence and samplingA field has area 800 m². Twenty 0.5 m² quadrats contain a total of 150 clover plants. Fewer clover plants are found near a shaded hedge. Estimate the total number of clover plants in the field.

questions.prompt: Interdependence and samplingA field has area 800 m². Twenty 0.5 m² quadrats contain a total of 150 clover plants. Fewer clover plants are found near a shaded hedge. Explain why the association with shade does not prove that light is the only cause.
scheme: 1 · Other factors may vary with distance (1).

questions.prompt: Carbon and water cyclesA restoration project plants 400 trees. In a simplified model, each tree removes an average of 12 kg carbon dioxide per year. scheme: 1 · Evaporation from sea/land and transpiration from plants move water into air (1).

questions.prompt: Carbon and water cyclesA restoration project plants 400 trees. In a simplified model, each tree removes an average of 12 kg carbon dioxide per year. In practice, the value varies with tree age and environmental conditions. Explain how deforestation can increase atmospheric carbon dioxide.
scheme: 1 · Fewer trees remove carbon dioxide by photosynthesis (1).

scheme: 2 · Gains one electron for a full outer shell (1).

questions.prompt: Isotopes and electronic structureA sample of element X contains 75% atoms of mass 35 and 25% atoms of mass 37. Every atom of X has 17 protons. Explain why chlorine is more reactive than bromine.
scheme: 1 · Chlorine has fewer shells/less shielding so incoming electron is closer to nucleus (1).

questions.prompt: Comparing giant structuresDiamond, graphite and silicon dioxide have giant covalent structures. Explain why diamond is hard and has a high melting point.

scheme: 1 · Each carbon has three covalent bonds, leaving delocalised electrons (1).

Comparing giant structuresDiamond, graphite and silicon dioxide have giant covalent structures. Explain why a small molecule such as methane has a lower melting point than silicon dioxide.
scheme: 1 · Only weak intermolecular forces need overcoming in methane (1).
2 · Strong covalent bonds throughout silicon dioxide require much more energy to break (1).

A second experiment gives a lower measured solid mass than predicted. Suggest one experimental cause and explain why it gives a lower value. Explain why this is not failure of conservation of mass.

scheme: 1 · Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻ → Cu; correct reactants including 2 electrons (1).

questions.prompt: Preparing a salt safelyA technician needs crystals of zinc sulfate from zinc oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Write a balanced symbol equation for the reaction.

scheme: 1 · Wear eye protection and warm dilute acid gently without boiling.

scheme: 1 · Clamp spring securely next to a vertical ruler and measure unloaded length.
