questions.prompt: A student uses a light microscope to observe onion epidermis cells stained with iodine. Explain why the onion tissue must be a single, thin layer of cells.
scheme: 1 · So light can pass through it (1)
2 · So individual cells can be seen clearly / cells do not overlap (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses a light microscope to observe onion epidermis cells stained with iodine. Describe how the student should focus on the cells.
scheme: 1 · Start with the lowest-power objective lens (1)
2 · Use the coarse focus to bring the stage close, then move away until the image is in focus (1)
3 · Use the fine focus, then switch to a higher power and refocus with fine focus (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses a light microscope to observe onion epidermis cells stained with iodine. A cell measures 24 mm in the student’s drawing at × 400. Calculate its real length in micrometres.
A student uses a light microscope to observe onion epidermis cells stained with iodine. Give two features of a good biological drawing.
scheme: 1 · Clear, continuous lines with no shading (1)
2 · Labels with straight lines / a title and magnification stated (1)

questions.prompt: A student puts potato cylinders into sucrose solutions of different concentrations for 30 minutes and measures their change in mass. A cylinder changes from 2.50 g to 2.20 g. Calculate the percentage change in mass.
A student puts potato cylinders into sucrose solutions of different concentrations for 30 minutes and measures their change in mass. Explain why the cylinder lost mass.
scheme: 1 · Solution is more concentrated than the potato cells (1)
2 · Water moves out of the cells by osmosis (1)
3 · Through the partially permeable cell membrane (1)

questions.prompt: A student puts potato cylinders into sucrose solutions of different concentrations for 30 minutes and measures their change in mass. Give two variables that should be controlled.
scheme: 1 · Size/length/surface area of cylinders (1)
2 · Time in solution / temperature / same potato (1)

questions.prompt: A student puts potato cylinders into sucrose solutions of different concentrations for 30 minutes and measures their change in mass. Describe how the student could use a graph of the results to estimate the concentration of the potato cell contents.
scheme: 1 · Plot percentage change in mass against concentration (1)
2 · Draw a line of best fit (1)
3 · Read off the concentration where the line crosses 0% (1)

questions.prompt: A student tests a sample of milk for sugar, starch, protein and lipid. Describe how to test the milk for reducing sugar and give the positive result.
scheme: 1 · Add Benedict’s solution (1)
2 · Heat in a water bath at about 75 °C for a few minutes (1)
3 · Colour change from blue to green/yellow/brick-red (1)

questions.prompt: A student tests a sample of milk for sugar, starch, protein and lipid. Name the reagent used to test for protein and the positive colour.
scheme: 1 · Biuret reagent (1)
2 · Lilac/purple (1)

questions.prompt: A student tests a sample of milk for sugar, starch, protein and lipid. Give one safety precaution when testing for lipids with ethanol.
scheme: 1 · Keep ethanol away from flames / flammable (1)

questions.prompt: A student tests a sample of milk for sugar, starch, protein and lipid. The Benedict’s test gives a yellow colour. Explain why this test is described as semi-quantitative.
scheme: 1 · Colour indicates approximately how much sugar is present (1)
2 · But does not give an exact concentration (1)

questions.prompt: A student tests a sample of milk for sugar, starch, protein and lipid. Suggest how the student could make the sugar test more quantitative.
scheme: 1 · Compare with colours from glucose solutions of known concentration / colour standards (1)
2 · Or use a colorimeter (1)

benz.title: The effect of pH on amylase

questions.prompt: A student investigates the effect of pH on amylase. Starch and amylase are mixed with a buffer, and a drop is tested with iodine every 30 seconds. Explain why a buffer solution is added.
scheme: 1 · To keep the pH constant at a known value (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates the effect of pH on amylase. Starch and amylase are mixed with a buffer, and a drop is tested with iodine every 30 seconds. At pH 6, iodine stopped turning blue-black after 150 s. Calculate the rate using rate = 1000 ÷ time.

A student investigates the effect of pH on amylase. Starch and amylase are mixed with a buffer, and a drop is tested with iodine every 30 seconds. Explain why sampling every 30 seconds limits the precision of the result.
scheme: 1 · The end point could be anywhere within the 30 s interval (1)
2 · Sample more often, e.g. every 10 s (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates the effect of pH on amylase. Starch and amylase are mixed with a buffer, and a drop is tested with iodine every 30 seconds. Give two control variables.
scheme: 1 · Temperature (water bath) (1)
2 · Volume/concentration of starch or amylase (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates the effect of pH on amylase. Starch and amylase are mixed with a buffer, and a drop is tested with iodine every 30 seconds. Explain why the rate is very low at pH 2.
scheme: 1 · Extreme pH changes the shape of the active site (1)
2 · Enzyme denatured (1)
3 · Starch no longer fits / fewer enzyme–substrate complexes form (1)

questions.prompt: Pondweed is placed at different distances from a lamp and the volume of oxygen collected in 5 minutes is measured. At 10 cm, 2.5 cm³ of oxygen is collected in 5 minutes. Calculate the rate in cm³/min.
scheme: 2 · 0.5 cm³/min (1)

questions.prompt: Pondweed is placed at different distances from a lamp and the volume of oxygen collected in 5 minutes is measured. Explain why the rate of photosynthesis decreases as the lamp is moved further away.
scheme: 1 · Light intensity decreases (1)
2 · Light is the limiting factor (1)

questions.prompt: Pondweed is placed at different distances from a lamp and the volume of oxygen collected in 5 minutes is measured. Describe how the student could keep the temperature constant.
scheme: 1 · Place the boiling tube in a water bath / use a heat shield or LED lamp (1)
2 · Monitor temperature with a thermometer (1)

questions.prompt: Pondweed is placed at different distances from a lamp and the volume of oxygen collected in 5 minutes is measured. Light intensity is proportional to 1/d². Calculate the relative light intensity at 20 cm compared with 10 cm.
scheme: 2 · 0.25 / one quarter (1)

questions.prompt: Pondweed is placed at different distances from a lamp and the volume of oxygen collected in 5 minutes is measured. Give one reason why collecting gas is better than counting bubbles.
scheme: 1 · Bubbles may be different sizes (1)
2 · Gas collection measures volume directly, so more accurate (1)

questions.prompt: Students use a ruler-drop test to compare reaction times with the dominant and non-dominant hand. Give the independent and dependent variables.
scheme: 1 · Independent: hand used (1)
2 · Dependent: distance the ruler falls / reaction time (1)

questions.prompt: Students use a ruler-drop test to compare reaction times with the dominant and non-dominant hand. Mean catch distances were 14 cm (dominant) and 19 cm (non-dominant). Calculate the percentage difference compared with the dominant hand.
Students use a ruler-drop test to compare reaction times with the dominant and non-dominant hand. Explain why the person dropping the ruler should not give a warning.
scheme: 1 · The catcher could anticipate the drop (1)
2 · So the measured value would not be a true reaction time (1)

questions.prompt: Students use a ruler-drop test to compare reaction times with the dominant and non-dominant hand. Suggest why the students should repeat each test several times.
scheme: 1 · To reduce the effect of random variation / practice effects (1)
2 · Identify anomalies and calculate a mean (1)

questions.prompt: Students use a ruler-drop test to compare reaction times with the dominant and non-dominant hand. Explain how the nervous system is involved in catching the ruler.
scheme: 1 · Receptors in the eye detect the falling ruler; impulses pass along sensory neurones to the brain (1)
2 · Impulses along motor neurones to hand muscles, which contract (1)

questions.prompt: Students investigate how the number of dandelions changes with distance from a hedge using a transect. Describe how the students should use the transect.
scheme: 1 · Lay a tape measure from the hedge across the field (1)
2 · Place a quadrat at regular intervals along the tape (1)
3 · Count dandelions in each quadrat (1)

questions.prompt: Students investigate how the number of dandelions changes with distance from a hedge using a transect. Name one abiotic factor they could measure at each quadrat and the equipment used.
scheme: 1 · Light intensity (1)
2 · Light meter (1); accept soil moisture with a moisture meter, temperature with a thermometer

questions.prompt: Students investigate how the number of dandelions changes with distance from a hedge using a transect. In another part of the field, mean dandelions per 0.25 m² quadrat is 1.5. The area is 600 m². Estimate the number of dandelions.
Students investigate how the number of dandelions changes with distance from a hedge using a transect. Explain why repeating the transect in different places improves the investigation.
scheme: 1 · Results more representative of the whole field (1)
2 · Reduces the effect of an unusual area / allows a mean (1)

questions.prompt: A student makes crystals of copper sulfate from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Explain why the acid is warmed and the copper oxide is added until no more dissolves.
scheme: 1 · Warming speeds up the reaction (1)
2 · Excess ensures all the acid reacts (1)

questions.prompt: A student makes crystals of copper sulfate from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Describe how the excess copper oxide is removed.
scheme: 1 · Filtration (1)

questions.prompt: A student makes crystals of copper sulfate from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Describe how to obtain pure, dry crystals from the solution.
scheme: 1 · Heat the solution gently in an evaporating basin to evaporate some water (1)
2 · Leave to cool so crystals form (1)
3 · Pat crystals dry with filter paper / leave in a warm place (1)

questions.prompt: A student makes crystals of copper sulfate from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Write the word equation for the reaction.
scheme: 1 · copper oxide + sulfuric acid → (1)
2 · copper sulfate + water (1)

questions.prompt: A student makes crystals of copper sulfate from copper oxide and dilute sulfuric acid. Give one hazard and how to reduce the risk.
scheme: 1 · Hot acid/solution can scald or spit (1)
2 · Wear eye protection / do not boil to dryness / heat gently (1)

questions.prompt: A student electrolyses aqueous solutions using inert carbon electrodes and identifies the products. Explain why the electrodes should be inert.
scheme: 1 · So they do not react with the products/electrolyte (1)

questions.prompt: A student electrolyses aqueous solutions using inert carbon electrodes and identifies the products. Copper chloride solution is electrolysed. Name the products at the cathode and anode.
scheme: 1 · Cathode: copper (1)
2 · Anode: chlorine (1)

questions.prompt: A student electrolyses aqueous solutions using inert carbon electrodes and identifies the products. Describe the test for chlorine.
scheme: 1 · Damp (blue) litmus paper (1)
2 · Is bleached / turns white (1)

questions.prompt: A student electrolyses aqueous solutions using inert carbon electrodes and identifies the products. Sodium chloride solution is electrolysed. Explain why hydrogen, not sodium, forms at the cathode.
scheme: 1 · Sodium is more reactive than hydrogen (1)
2 · H⁺ ions from water are discharged instead (1)
3 · 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → H₂ / hydrogen gas forms (1)

questions.prompt: A student electrolyses aqueous solutions using inert carbon electrodes and identifies the products. Give a safety precaution and the reason for it.
scheme: 1 · Use low voltage / do in a well-ventilated room (1)
2 · Chlorine is toxic / to avoid electric shock (1)

questions.prompt: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution in 5 cm³ portions to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup and records the highest temperature after each addition. Explain why a polystyrene cup with a lid is used.
scheme: 1 · Polystyrene is a good insulator (1)
2 · Reduces energy transfer to the surroundings (1)

questions.prompt: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution in 5 cm³ portions to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup and records the highest temperature after each addition. Starting temperature 19.5 °C; maximum 28.3 °C. Calculate the temperature rise.

A student adds sodium hydroxide solution in 5 cm³ portions to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup and records the highest temperature after each addition. Is the reaction exothermic or endothermic? Explain.
scheme: 1 · Exothermic (1)
2 · Temperature of surroundings/solution increases (1)

questions.prompt: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution in 5 cm³ portions to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup and records the highest temperature after each addition. Explain why the temperature falls when more alkali is added after neutralisation is complete.
scheme: 1 · No more reaction, so no more energy released (1)
2 · Cooler alkali added / energy lost to surroundings (1)

questions.prompt: A student adds sodium hydroxide solution in 5 cm³ portions to 25 cm³ of hydrochloric acid in a polystyrene cup and records the highest temperature after each addition. Suggest how to improve the accuracy of the temperature readings.
scheme: 1 · Use a digital thermometer/probe with higher resolution (1)
2 · Stir the mixture (1)
3 · Repeat and calculate means / use smaller volume intervals near the maximum (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how the concentration of sodium thiosulfate affects the rate of its reaction with hydrochloric acid by timing how long it takes for a cross under the flask to disappear. Explain why the cross disappears.
scheme: 1 · A precipitate of sulfur forms, making the solution cloudy (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how the concentration of sodium thiosulfate affects the rate of its reaction with hydrochloric acid by timing how long it takes for a cross under the flask to disappear. At one concentration the cross disappears after 50 s. Calculate the rate as 1/time.

A student investigates how the concentration of sodium thiosulfate affects the rate of its reaction with hydrochloric acid by timing how long it takes for a cross under the flask to disappear. Explain, using collision theory, why increasing the concentration increases the rate.
scheme: 1 · More particles in the same volume (1)
2 · More frequent collisions (1)
3 · More successful collisions per second (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how the concentration of sodium thiosulfate affects the rate of its reaction with hydrochloric acid by timing how long it takes for a cross under the flask to disappear. Give two control variables.
scheme: 1 · Volume/concentration of acid (1)
2 · Temperature / same cross / same total volume (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how the concentration of sodium thiosulfate affects the rate of its reaction with hydrochloric acid by timing how long it takes for a cross under the flask to disappear. Suggest one improvement and explain why it would reduce error.
scheme: 1 · Use a light sensor/data logger (1)
2 · Removes subjective judgement of when the cross disappears (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses paper chromatography to identify the dyes in a food colouring. Explain why the start line is drawn in pencil, not ink.
scheme: 1 · Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent (1)
2 · Ink would separate and interfere with results (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses paper chromatography to identify the dyes in a food colouring. Explain why the start line must be above the level of the solvent.
scheme: 1 · So the dyes do not dissolve into the solvent in the beaker (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses paper chromatography to identify the dyes in a food colouring. A dye spot moves 4.2 cm; the solvent front moves 7.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value.
A student uses paper chromatography to identify the dyes in a food colouring. The food colouring produced three spots. What does this tell you?
scheme: 1 · It is a mixture (1)
2 · Of at least three dyes / it is impure (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses paper chromatography to identify the dyes in a food colouring. Explain how the student could identify one of the dyes.
scheme: 1 · Run known dyes on the same paper (1)
2 · Compare Rf values / heights of spots (1)
3 · Matching Rf in the same solvent shows the same dye (1)

questions.prompt: A student analyses and purifies a sample of salty water. Describe how to find the mass of dissolved solids in 50 cm³ of the sample.
scheme: 1 · Weigh an empty evaporating basin (1)
2 · Add 50 cm³ of sample and heat until all water evaporates (1)
3 · Reweigh; difference = mass of solids (1)

questions.prompt: A student analyses and purifies a sample of salty water. The solid had a mass of 1.75 g. Calculate the concentration of dissolved solids in g/dm³.
A student analyses and purifies a sample of salty water. Describe how distillation produces pure water from the sample.
scheme: 1 · Heat the water so it evaporates (1)
2 · Steam passes into a condenser and cools (1)
3 · Water condenses and is collected; salts remain (1)

questions.prompt: A student analyses and purifies a sample of salty water. Describe how to test that the distilled water is pure.
scheme: 1 · Measure its boiling point (1)
2 · Pure water boils at exactly 100 °C (1)

questions.prompt: A student heats a 1.0 kg aluminium block with a 50 W electric heater and records its temperature every minute. Calculate the energy supplied by the heater in 10 minutes.
A student heats a 1.0 kg aluminium block with a 50 W electric heater and records its temperature every minute. The temperature rose by 32 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium.
scheme: 1 · c = ΔE ÷ (m Δθ) (1)

questions.prompt: A student heats a 1.0 kg aluminium block with a 50 W electric heater and records its temperature every minute. The accepted value is 900 J/kg °C. Explain why the student’s value is higher.
scheme: 1 · Energy lost to the surroundings (1)
2 · So not all energy supplied raised the block’s temperature (1)

questions.prompt: A student heats a 1.0 kg aluminium block with a 50 W electric heater and records its temperature every minute. Suggest two improvements to the method.
scheme: 1 · Insulate the block (1)
2 · Put oil in the thermometer hole for good thermal contact / use a joulemeter (1)

questions.prompt: A student heats a 1.0 kg aluminium block with a 50 W electric heater and records its temperature every minute. Explain why the thermometer reading continues to rise after the heater is switched off.
scheme: 1 · Heater is still hot and transfers energy to the block (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how the length of a wire affects its resistance. Draw or describe the circuit used.
scheme: 1 · Ammeter in series with the wire (1)
2 · Voltmeter in parallel with the wire (1)
3 · Battery/power supply with crocodile clips to vary length (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how the length of a wire affects its resistance. At 50 cm, V = 1.8 V and I = 0.30 A. Calculate the resistance.
A student investigates how the length of a wire affects its resistance. Explain why the current should be kept small.
scheme: 1 · Large current heats the wire (1)
2 · Increasing resistance / temperature becomes another variable (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how the length of a wire affects its resistance. The graph of resistance against length is a straight line that does not pass through the origin. Suggest a reason.
scheme: 1 · Zero error / resistance of connecting wires and clips / contact resistance (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how the length of a wire affects its resistance. Describe the relationship between length and resistance shown by a straight line through the origin.
scheme: 1 · Resistance is directly proportional to length (1)
2 · Doubling length doubles resistance (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates the I–V characteristics of a filament lamp, a resistor and a diode. Describe how the student changes the potential difference and gets negative values.
scheme: 1 · Use a variable resistor / variable power supply (1)
2 · Reverse the connections to the component (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates the I–V characteristics of a filament lamp, a resistor and a diode. Describe the shape of the I–V graph for a filament lamp and explain it.
scheme: 1 · Curve: gradient decreases as V increases (1)
2 · Filament gets hotter as current increases (1)
3 · So resistance increases (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates the I–V characteristics of a filament lamp, a resistor and a diode. A diode has a current of 0.020 A at 0.70 V. Calculate its resistance.
A student investigates the I–V characteristics of a filament lamp, a resistor and a diode. Describe the I–V graph of a diode.
scheme: 1 · No/very small current in the reverse direction (1)
2 · Current increases sharply above about 0.6–0.7 V in forward direction (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates the I–V characteristics of a filament lamp, a resistor and a diode. Explain why a resistor at constant temperature is described as ohmic.
scheme: 1 · Current is directly proportional to potential difference / straight line through origin (1)

questions.prompt: A student measures the density of a stone and of a wooden block. The wooden block is 5.0 cm × 4.0 cm × 3.0 cm and has a mass of 42 g. Calculate its density in g/cm³.
scheme: 1 · Volume = 60 cm³ (1)

questions.prompt: A student measures the density of a stone and of a wooden block. Describe how to find the volume of the irregular stone.
scheme: 1 · Fill a displacement (eureka) can to the spout (1)
2 · Lower the stone in and collect the displaced water in a measuring cylinder (1)
3 · Volume of water = volume of stone (1)

questions.prompt: A student measures the density of a stone and of a wooden block. Convert 0.70 g/cm³ to kg/m³.
A student measures the density of a stone and of a wooden block. Suggest two sources of error when measuring the stone’s volume.
scheme: 1 · Water drips from spout after collection / water left in the can spout (1)
2 · Reading the measuring cylinder (meniscus) / bubbles on stone (1)

questions.prompt: A student measures the density of a stone and of a wooden block. Explain how the student could make the volume measurement more precise.
scheme: 1 · Use a measuring cylinder with smaller divisions / smaller cylinder (1)

questions.prompt: A student hangs masses on a spring and measures its extension. A force of 4.0 N gives an extension of 0.050 m. Calculate the spring constant.
A student hangs masses on a spring and measures its extension. Explain why the student should read the ruler at eye level with a pointer.
scheme: 1 · Avoids parallax error (1)
2 · So length readings are accurate (1)

questions.prompt: A student hangs masses on a spring and measures its extension. Describe what the graph of force against extension shows if the limit of proportionality is exceeded.
scheme: 1 · Line stops being straight / curves (1)
2 · Extension is no longer proportional to force (1)

questions.prompt: A student hangs masses on a spring and measures its extension. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored when the spring is extended by 0.050 m.
A student hangs masses on a spring and measures its extension. Give one safety precaution.
scheme: 1 · Clamp the stand to the bench / use a counterweight (1)
2 · Wear eye protection / keep feet away from falling masses (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how force affects the acceleration of a trolley using light gates. The trolley’s speed changes from 0.20 m/s to 0.80 m/s in 0.50 s. Calculate the acceleration.
A student investigates how force affects the acceleration of a trolley using light gates. Explain why masses are moved from the trolley to the hanger to increase the force.
scheme: 1 · Keeps the total mass of the system constant (1)
2 · So only the force changes / fair test (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how force affects the acceleration of a trolley using light gates. Explain why light gates give better results than a stopwatch.
scheme: 1 · No human reaction time (1)
2 · Can measure short times precisely / reduces random error (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how force affects the acceleration of a trolley using light gates. State the relationship the student should find between force and acceleration.
scheme: 1 · Acceleration is directly proportional to resultant force (1)

questions.prompt: A student investigates how force affects the acceleration of a trolley using light gates. Suggest how the student could compensate for friction.
scheme: 1 · Tilt the runway slightly (1)
2 · Until the trolley moves at constant speed when pushed (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses a ripple tank to measure the speed of water waves. Describe how to measure the wavelength.
scheme: 1 · Use a ruler on the shadow pattern / photograph with a scale (1)
2 · Measure across several waves and divide by the number of waves (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses a ripple tank to measure the speed of water waves. 10 waves pass a point in 4.0 s. Calculate the frequency.
A student uses a ripple tank to measure the speed of water waves. The wavelength is 0.018 m. Calculate the wave speed.
A student uses a ripple tank to measure the speed of water waves. Explain why measuring across ten waves gives a more accurate wavelength.
scheme: 1 · Measurement uncertainty is spread over 10 waves (1)
2 · Smaller percentage error per wavelength (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses a ripple tank to measure the speed of water waves. Give one way of measuring the speed of waves on a string.
scheme: 1 · Vibration generator and signal generator; measure λ with a metre rule (1)
2 · Read f from the signal generator and use v = fλ (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses a Leslie cube with four different surfaces filled with hot water and an infrared detector. Give the independent and dependent variables.
scheme: 1 · Independent: type of surface (1)
2 · Dependent: infrared radiation emitted / detector reading (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses a Leslie cube with four different surfaces filled with hot water and an infrared detector. Predict which surface emits the most infrared radiation.
scheme: 1 · Matt black (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses a Leslie cube with four different surfaces filled with hot water and an infrared detector. Explain why the detector should be the same distance from each surface.
scheme: 1 · Intensity depends on distance (1)
2 · So it is a fair test / only the surface affects the reading (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses a Leslie cube with four different surfaces filled with hot water and an infrared detector. Give one hazard and how to reduce the risk.
scheme: 1 · Hot water can scald (1)
2 · Do not touch the cube / fill carefully / wipe spills (1)

questions.prompt: A student uses a Leslie cube with four different surfaces filled with hot water and an infrared detector. Describe the order of the surfaces from best to worst emitter.
scheme: 1 · Matt black best (1)
2 · Shiny black / white next (1)
3 · Shiny silver worst (1)
